Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 57, verse 1:

(p-432) Surat "al-Hadid"

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Glorifies Allah﴾. In some of the opening surahs the verb "sabbaha" (glorified) occurs in the past tense, in some in the present tense, in "Bani Isra'il" in the verbal noun form (tasbih), and in "al-A'la" in the imperative, so as to encompass this word from all its aspects. These are four: the verbal noun (masdar), the past tense (madi), the present tense (mudari'), and the imperative (amr). This verb is transitive by the preposition lam at times and directly at other times, as in His words: ﴿and glorify Him﴾ [al-Fath: 9]. Its original form is transitive directly, because the meaning of "sabbahtuhu" (I declared Him far removed) is derived from "sabaha" (to go away and be far off), when one departs and distances oneself. So the lam is either like the lam in "nasahtuhu" and "nasahtu lahu" (I advised him), or it is intended that "sabbaha lillah" means: he acquired the glorification for the sake of Allah and for His face, sincerely.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾: whatever can be characterised by glorification and is fit for it.

﴿And He is the Almighty﴾: the Avenger against a responsible person who did not glorify Him out of obstinacy.

﴿the Wise﴾: in recompensing the one who glorified Him in submission.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 57, verse 2:

﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, not to anyone else. The place of ﴿يُحْيِي﴾ [Al-A'raf: 158] is in the nominative case (raf'), meaning: He gives life to the dead,

﴿and causes death﴾, to the living. Or it is in the accusative case (nasb), meaning: To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, giving life and causing death,

﴿and He is Able over all things﴾.

He is the First (al-Awwal): He is the Eternal (al-Qadim), who existed before everything.

And the Last (al-Akhir): He who remains after everything has perished.

And the Manifest (al-Zahir): through the proofs that point to Him.

And the Hidden (al-Batin): because He is not perceived by the senses, even though He can be seen [p. 433].

The first wa-w (the conjunction "and," wāw) indicates that He combines the two attributes of being First and being Last. The third wāw indicates that He combines manifestness and hiddenness. As for the middle wāw, it indicates that He combines the two pairs of attributes together: He is the one whose existence is continuous at all times, past and future, and He is manifest and hidden in all of them.

It has also been said: "al-Zahir" means the one who is exalted above everything and prevails over it, from "zahara 'alayhi," meaning when someone rises above another and overcomes him. And "al-Batin" means the one who knows the inner reality (batn) of everything, that is, He knows its inner aspect.

﴿And He is Knowing of all things.﴾

Surah 57, verse 6, from al-Nasafi's Madarik al-Tanzil:

﴿He causes the night to enter into the day﴾: He makes the night enter into the day, by the night decreasing and the day increasing.

﴿And He causes the day to enter into the night, and He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 57, verse 7:

﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾. It may mean zakat and spending in the way of Allah (sabil Allah).

﴿And spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾. That is, the wealth that is in your hands is in reality the wealth of Allah, by His creation and origination of it. He only provided it to you for you to enjoy it, and made you successors (khulafa') in disposing of it. So it is not in truth your property; you are in it only in the position of agents (wukala') and deputies (nuwwab). So spend from it in the rights of Allah (exalted is He). Let spending from it be easy for you, just as it is easy for a man to spend from another's property when that person has permitted him to do so. Or [it means]: He made you successors of those who were before you in what is in your hands, by having it inherited by you, and it will be transferred from you to those after you. So take heed from their condition, and do not be stingy with it.

﴿So those of you who believe﴾, in Allah and His Messenger,

﴿and spend, for them there is a great reward﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 57, verse 8:

﴿And what is the matter with you that you do not believe in Allah?﴾ This is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause, a grammatical state) relating to the sense of the verb in "mā lakum," just as you say: "Mā laka qā'iman?!" meaning: "What are you doing standing?!" That is: "And what is the matter with you, being disbelievers in Allah?!" The wāw in ﴿while the Messenger calls you﴾ is the wāw of ḥāl, so the two are interlinked circumstantial clauses, and the meaning is: "What excuse do you have for abandoning faith, while the Messenger is calling you?!"

﴿So that you may believe in your Lord, and He has already taken your covenant﴾. Before this, Allah had already taken your covenant by His saying: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ [al-A'raf: 172], or by what He placed in you of intellects and enabled you to reflect upon the proofs. So when no excuse remains for you after the proofs of reason and the Messenger's admonition, then what is the matter with you that you do not believe?! ﴿If you are believers﴾, by some compelling cause, for this compelling cause has no addition beyond it. "Akhadha mithaqakum" (your covenant was taken) is the reading of Abu 'Amr.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 57, verse 9:**

﴿He is the One who sends down upon His servant﴾, Muhammad (ﷺ),

﴿clear verses﴾, meaning the Qur'an,

﴿that He may bring you out﴾, Allah (exalted is He), or Muhammad, through his call,

﴿from darknesses into light﴾, from the darknesses of disbelief into the light of faith,

﴿And indeed Allah is, to you, Most Kind﴾, with the madd (lengthening of the vowel) and the hamza, "Hijazi, Shami, and Hafs" (the readings attributed to these readers),

﴿Merciful﴾, "al-ra'fah" (ٱلرَّأْفَةُ, tenderness), which is the more intense form of mercy.

[Surah 57, verse 10]

﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not spend⁠ ⁠—⁠ ⁠﴾ "that you do not spend" (أَلَّا تُنْفِقُوا) [here "ألّا" is "أن" with negation].

﴿in the way of Allah, while to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾: He inherits everything in them; nothing remains of it for anyone, of wealth or otherwise. The meaning is: what reason do you have for not spending in the way of Allah and for not striving (jihad) alongside His Messenger, when Allah is the one who will destroy you, and the inheritor of your wealth?! This is among the most forceful incitements to spend in the way of Allah. Then he clarified the difference between those among them who spend, saying:

﴿Not equal among you are those who spent before the conquest and fought⁠﴾: that is, the conquest of Mecca, before the might of Islam, the strength of its people, and the entry of people into the religion of Allah in multitudes. [And "those who spent after the conquest" is omitted, because His saying "from those who spent afterwards" indicates it.]

﴿Those⁠﴾ who spent before the conquest, and they are the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers, concerning whom the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If one of you spent the equivalent of Uhud in gold, it would not reach the mudd of one of them, nor half of it."

﴿Those are greater in rank than those who spent afterwards and fought.⁠﴾ And each [of the two groups]:

﴿Allah has promised the best⁠﴾ — that is, the best reward, which is Paradise — with differing degrees. "Kullan" is the first object of "wa'ada" (promised), and "al-husna" is the second object. "Wa-kullun" is read by the Syrian reciter, meaning: "and everyone Allah has promised the best." It was revealed concerning Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), because he was the first to embrace Islam and the first to spend in the way of Allah, and in it is evidence of his virtue and precedence.

﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do.⁠﴾ So He will recompense you according to the measure of your deeds.

﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan﴾, with a willing soul? The intended meaning is spending in His cause. The word "loan" (qard) is used figuratively (isti'ara) to indicate the binding obligation of reward.

﴿So He will multiply it for him﴾, that is, He will give him his reward for his spending multiplied many times over, out of His bounty.

﴿And he will have a generous reward﴾, that is, that reward, to which the multiples are added, is generous in itself. "فَيُضَعِّفُهُ" (fa-yuda'figuhu) is read by Makki, "فَيُضَعِّفَهُ" (fa-yuda'iffahu) by Shami, "فَيُضاعِفَهُ" (fa-yudaa'ifahu) by ʿAsim and Sahl, and "فَيُضاعِفُهُ" (fa-yudaa'ifuhu) by the others. The accusative (naṣb) reading is in response to the interrogative (as the answer to the question), while the nominative (rafʿ) reading is either "fa-huwa yudaa'ifuhu" (so He multiplies it), or a conjunction with "yuqriḍu" (lends).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 57, verse 12:

﴿The Day you will see the believing men and the believing women, their light running before them and on their right hands,﴾ is an adverbial clause (ẓarf) governed by his saying: "and for him is a generous reward," or it is in the accusative by the implied verb "remember" (udhkur), to magnify that day.

﴿Running﴾ means proceeding.

﴿Their light﴾ is the light of monotheism (tawhid) and of acts of obedience (ta'at). As for His saying: ﴿before them and on their right hands﴾, it is because the blessed are given their records of deeds from these two directions, just as the wretched are given them from their left hands and from behind their backs. So light is placed in both directions as their sign and token, because they are those whose good deeds made them blessed, or whose white records brought them success. When they are taken to Paradise and pass over the Sirat, they hasten, and the light moves along with their running. The angels say to them: ﴿Good news for you today: gardens,﴾ meaning entry into gardens, because good news falls upon the graves (ajdath), not upon the bodies (judhuth).

﴿Beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great triumph.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 57, verse 13:

﴿On the Day when﴾, it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the Day you will see﴾,

﴿the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women will say to those who believed: "Wait for us (unzurūnā)"﴾, i.e., wait for us (intaẓirūnā), because they will be hurried toward Paradise like lightning flashes. "Unẓirūnā" is the reading of Hamzah, from "al-nazrah" (al-naẓra), which means granting respite (al-imhāl). Their slowing down in going on, until they catch up with them, was made a granting of respite to them (in'ẓār),

﴿that we may borrow from your light﴾, the verb is in the subjunctive (naṣb) after it, and that is so that they may catch up with them and be illuminated by it,

﴿It will be said: "Return behind you and seek light"﴾, a rejection of them and a mockery of them, i.e., the angels, or the believers, will say to them: "Return to the place of standing (al-mawqif), where this light was given to us, and seek it there," for from there it is taken; or: "Return to the world, and seek by acquiring its cause, which is faith."

﴿So a wall will be set up between them﴾, between the believers and the hypocrites,

﴿with a gate﴾, a wall, dividing between the side of Paradise and the side of the Fire. It is said: it is al-A'raf.

﴿Its inner side﴾, for it (the wall),

﴿has a gate﴾, for the people of Paradise, through which they enter,

﴿its inner side﴾, the inner side of the wall, or of the gate, which is the side that faces Paradise,

﴿wherein is mercy﴾, i.e., the light, or Paradise,

﴿and its outer side﴾, what is apparent to the people of the Fire,

﴿is from before it﴾, from in front of it, and from its direction,

﴿the punishment﴾, i.e., the darkness, or the Fire.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 57, verse 14:

﴿Yunadunahum﴾: that is, the hypocrites (al-munafiqun) will call out to the believers (al-mu'minun),

﴿Alam nakun ma'akum?﴾ ("Were we not with you?"), meaning: accompanying them outwardly,

﴿Qalu﴾: that is, the believers will reply,

﴿Bala, wa lakinnakum fatantum anfusakum﴾ ("Yes, but you tempted yourselves"): you put them to trial (mahantumuha) by hypocrisy, and you destroyed them,

﴿Wa tarabbasttum﴾ ("and you waited"): for the believers, the misfortunes (al-dawa'ir),

﴿Wa irtabtum﴾ ("and you doubted"): and you were skeptical about (p-437) the Tawhid (divine oneness),

﴿Wa gharrat-kumu al-amani﴾ ("and false hopes deceived you"): the prolonging of hopes and the greed for the extension of lifespans,

﴿Hatta ja'a amru Allah﴾ ("until the command of Allah came"): that is, death,

﴿Wa gharrakum bi-Allahi al-gharur﴾ ("and the Deceiver deceived you concerning Allah"): the Shaytan (Satan) deceived you into thinking that Allah is Forgiving and Generous, that He will not punish you, or that there is no resurrection and no reckoning.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 57, verse 15:

﴿Today no ransom will be taken﴾ — with the taʾ (in yuʾkhadhu read as tuʾkhadhu), read by "al-Shamiyy" (Ibn ʿĀmir, the Syrian reader),

﴿from you﴾, O hypocrites,

﴿ransom﴾, that by which one may ransom oneself,

﴿nor from those who disbelieved. Your refuge is the Fire﴾, your place of return,

﴿it is your mawlā﴾, it is more deserving of you. The literal meaning of "mawlākum" is "maḥrākum" (your place of turning, the place where one is said to be), meaning: your place, of which it is said: "It is more deserving of you," just as it is said: "He is a mazinnah for generosity," meaning: a place for the saying of the speaker: "Indeed he is generous,"

﴿and wretched is the destination﴾, the Fire.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 57, verse 16:

﴿Has not the time come﴾, from "anā al-amr, yaʾnī" (the matter arrived), meaning: when its appointed time (inān, waqt) has come. It was said: they were in barren conditions in Mecca, but when they emigrated they obtained provision and blessing, and so they slackened from what they had been upon. Therefore it was revealed.

It is narrated from Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him: "There was no more than four years between our accepting Islam and being reproached with this verse."

And it is narrated from Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, that this verse was recited in his presence, and with him were some people from the people of Yamama, and they wept intensely. He looked at them and said: "So were we, until the hearts hardened."

﴿for those who believe, that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of Allah and to what has descended of the truth﴾, [i.e., the Qur'an], because it combines both matters: the remembrance (dhikr) and the admonition (mawʿiza), and because it is the truth, descended from the heaven. "And be not like those who were given the Scripture before, and the term grew long for them" — the reading with the ya' (yāʾ) is a conjunction upon "takhshaʿa" (that they should humble themselves), and with the taʾ (tāʾ) it is Warsh's reading, by way of iltifat (shift of address). It is permissible that it be a prohibition to them against resembling the People of the Book in hardness of heart, after they had been rebuked. That is because the Children of Israel, the truth would stand between them and their desires, and when they heard the Torah (p-438) and the Gospel they humbled themselves to Allah and their hearts softened. But when time lengthened over them, harshness and hardness overcame them, they differed, and they introduced what they introduced of distortion and other things.

﴿So the term grew long for them﴾: the appointed time and the duration.

﴿So their hearts hardened﴾: by following their desires.

﴿And many of them are defiant transgressors﴾: going out from their religion, rejecting what is in the two Books. That is: and few of them are believers.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 57, verse 17:

﴿Know that Allah gives life to the earth after its death. We have indeed made the signs clear to you, so that you may understand.﴾ It is said: this is an illustration (tamthil) of the effect of remembrance (dhikr) upon the hearts, and that it gives them life just as rain (ghayth) gives life to the earth.

"Indeed, those who give charity (al-muṣaddiqīn) and those who give charity (al-muṣaddiqāt)", with the dal doubled, is read by Makki and Abu Bakr. It is an active participle from ṣaddaqa, and they are those who believed in Allah and His Messenger, meaning the believers. The rest read it with the ṣad and dal both doubled, an active participle from taṣaddaqa, where the taʾ is assimilated into the ṣad. It is also read according to the original form.

﴿And lend to Allah a goodly loan﴾ is a conjunction over the sense of the verb in "al-muṣaddiqīn", because the lam is in the sense of "alladhīna" (those who), and the active participle carries the sense of the verb, which is "taṣaddaqū" (they gave charity). It is as if it were said: "Indeed those who gave charity and lent". "The goodly loan" (al-qarḍ al-ḥasan) is that one gives charity from what is good, willingly and with sincere intention, to one who deserves charity.

﴿It will be multiplied for them﴾, read "yuḍʿaf" (with the ʿayn doubled) by Makki and the Syrian reader.

﴿And for them is a noble reward﴾, that is, Paradise.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 57, verse 19:

﴿And those who believe in Allah and His messengers—those are the ṣiddīqūn (the truthful, those of utmost sincerity) and the shuhadā' (the martyrs) with their Lord.﴾ He means: those who believe in Allah and His messengers are, in the sight of Allah, in the rank of the ṣiddīqīn and the shuhadā'. They are those who were foremost in affirming (the truth), and who were martyred in the way of Allah.

﴿For them is their reward and their light.﴾ That is: the like of the reward of the ṣiddīqīn and the shuhadā', and the like of their light. It is also permissible for "wa-l-shuhadā'" to be a subject (mubtada'), and "lahum (p-439) ajruhum" its predicate (khabar).

﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs—those are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾

﴿Know that the life of this world is but play﴾, like the play of children,

﴿and amusement﴾, like the amusement of youths,

﴿and adornment﴾, like the adornment of women,

﴿and boasting among yourselves﴾, like the boasting of peers,

﴿and rivalry in increase﴾, like the rivalry of the landowners (al-dihqan),

﴿in wealth and children﴾, meaning: vying with one another in them. And "al-takathur" (rivalry in increase) means claiming to have much.

﴿Like the likeness of rain, whose growth pleases the disbelievers, then it dries up and you see it turning yellow﴾, after its greenness,

﴿then it becomes debris﴾, crumbled to pieces. He likened the state of this world, the swiftness of its passing, together with its little benefit, to a plant that the rain has caused to grow, which then becomes full-grown and strong, and which the disbelievers, those who deny the blessing of God in what He has provided them of rain and vegetation, admire. Then He sends a blight upon it, so it withers and turns yellow and becomes debris, as a punishment for them for their denial, just as He did to the people of the garden and the owner of the two gardens. It is also said that "al-kuffar" (the disbelievers) here means the farmers.

﴿And in the Hereafter there is severe punishment, and forgiveness from God and approval, and the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion﴾.

﴿And in the Hereafter there is severe punishment﴾, for the disbelievers,

﴿and forgiveness from God and approval﴾, for the believers. The meaning is that this world and what is in it are only among trivial matters, namely play, amusement, adornment, boasting and rivalry in increase, whereas the Hereafter consists of momentous matters: the severe punishment, and the forgiveness and approval from God, the Praiseworthy. The kaf in "kamathali ghaythin" (like the likeness of rain) is in a place of raising (nominative case), as it is a predicate following a predicate, meaning: the life of this world is like rain.

﴿And the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion﴾, if one relies upon it and depends upon it. Dhu al-Nun said: "O assembly of seekers, do not pursue this world, and if you pursue it, do not love it, for provision is from it, and resting place is in other than it." When He belittled this world and minimized its matter, and magnified the matter of the Hereafter, He urged His servants to hasten toward attaining what He promised of that, namely the forgiveness that saves from the severe punishment and the success of entering Paradise, by His saying:

Race (sābiqū), that is, through righteous deeds,

﴿to forgiveness from your Lord﴾. It was also said: hasten with the haste of those who outrun their rivals on the racecourse (al-midmār),

﴿and a Garden whose breadth is like the breadth of the heavens and the earth﴾. Al-Suddī said: "Like the breadth of the seven heavens and the seven earths." (p-٤٤٠) He mentioned the breadth and not the length, because everything that has breadth and length has a breadth less than its length. So when its breadth is described as spaciousness, it is known that its length is even more spacious. Or, by breadth is meant spaciousness. This refutes the view of those who say that Paradise is in the fourth heaven, because that which is in one of the heavens cannot have the breadth of the heavens and the earth.

﴿prepared for those who believe in God and His messengers﴾. This is evidence that it has already been created.

﴿That﴾, the promised forgiveness and Garden,

﴿is the bounty of God, which He gives to whom He wills﴾. They are the believers. This is evidence that no one enters Paradise except by the bounty of God.

﴿And God is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾ Then He explained that every existing thing occurs by the decree and predestination of God, in His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 57, verse 22:

﴿No affliction befalls [anyone] on the earth﴾, such as drought and blights of crops and fruits. His saying "on the earth" is in the genitive position, meaning: no affliction that is established on the earth befalls [anyone],

﴿nor in yourselves﴾, such as illnesses, ailments, and the death of children,

﴿but it is in a Book﴾, in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh), and it is in the accusative position of circumstance (al-hal), meaning: "but it is written in the Tablet,"

﴿before We bring it into being﴾, before We create the souls,

﴿Indeed that﴾, indeed the decreeing of that and its recording in a Book,

﴿for Allah is easy﴾, even though it is difficult for the servants. Then he gave the reason for that and explained its wisdom, by his saying:

﴿So that you may not grieve﴾ over what has escaped you, i.e., you should not grieve to the point of transgression (yutghikum),

﴿over what has escaped you﴾, from the world and its abundance, or from health and well-being;

﴿and do not exult﴾ with the exultation of the arrogant and boastful,

﴿in what He has given you﴾. "Ataakum" (He has given you) is from "al-ita'" (giving); Abu 'Amr read "ataakum" (He has come to you), meaning "jaa'akum" (has come to you), from "al-itiyan" (coming). The meaning is: when you know that everything is predetermined and written with Allah, your grief over what has passed will diminish and your joy over what comes will be lessened, because whoever knows that what he possesses is inevitably going to be lost does not excessively lament its loss, since he has prepared his soul for that. Likewise, whoever knows that some good will reach him, and that its arrival will by no means escape him, does not greatly rejoice when he attains it. No one is free of rejoicing when a benefit befalls him, or of grief when a harm descends upon him (p-441). Yet it is fitting that joy be gratitude and grief be patience. Only that grief is blameworthy which is excessive lamentation contrary to patience, and only that joy is blameworthy which is insolent pride that transgresses and distracts from gratitude.

﴿And Allah does not love every arrogant boaster﴾, because whoever rejoices in a portion of the world and it becomes great in his soul, he becomes arrogant, boastful, and haughty towards people.

﴿Those who are miserly﴾: a predicate (khabar, the complement of the subject) of an omitted subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject), or a substitute (badal, an apposition) for ﴿every arrogant boaster﴾. It is as if he had said: "He does not love those who are miserly." He means: those who rejoice with an exulting joy when they are given wealth and a share of this world. Because of their love for it and their esteem for it in their hearts, they withhold it from the rights of God and are miserly with it.

﴿And they enjoin people to miserliness﴾: they urge others toward miserliness and encourage them to withhold.

﴿And whoever turns away﴾: he turns away from spending, or from the commands and prohibitions of God, and does not desist from what He has forbidden, through grief over what has passed and joy over what has come.

﴿Indeed, God is the Self-Sufficient﴾: free of all creatures, so how could He need them? ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾: in His actions.

"Indeed God is the Self-Sufficient" (فَإنَّ اللهَ الغَنِيُّ), without the word "huwa" (هُوَ, "He"), is the reading of the Madani (the people of Medina) and the Shami (the people of Syria) readers.

﴿Indeed We sent Our messengers﴾, meaning: We sent the angels to the prophets,

﴿with clear proofs﴾, with arguments and miracles,

﴿and sent down with them the Book﴾, that is, the revelation. It was also said that "the Book" refers to the messengers, the prophets. The first view is preferable, because of His saying "with them," since the Book is sent down upon the prophets.

﴿and the Balance﴾. It is related that Jibril (Gabriel) descended with the Balance, gave it to Nuh (Noah), and said: "Command your people to weigh with it."

﴿That people may maintain justice﴾, so that they may deal with one another in giving and taking,

﴿with equity﴾, with justice, and that no one may wrong another.

﴿And We sent down iron﴾. It was said that Adam descended from the Garden with five iron tools: the sandan (anvil), the kalbatan (tongs), the miqa'a (hammer block), the mitraqa (hammer), and the ibra (needle). It is also related that with him were the marr (a cutting tool) and the mishaq (a tool for polishing). From al-Hasan: "﴿And We sent down iron﴾" means "We created it."

﴿in which is great might﴾, namely, fighting with it.

﴿and benefits for mankind﴾, in their interests, their livelihoods, and their crafts. There is no craft in which iron is not an instrument, or something made of iron.

﴿And that Allah may know who supports Him and His messengers﴾ (p-٤٤٢) by employing swords, spears, and all kinds of weapons in striving against the enemies of the religion. Al-Zajjaj said: "That Allah may know who fights alongside His messenger in His cause, unseen by them (the messengers)."

﴿Indeed, Allah is Powerful﴾, He repels by His power the might of whoever turns away from His religion,

﴿Mighty﴾, He binds by His might the heart of whoever opposes His support. The connection among these three things is that the Book is the law of the Sharia and the constitution of the rulings and limits; it commands justice and goodness and forbids transgression and tyranny. The practice of justice and the avoidance of wrong occur only through an instrument by which dealing is carried out and by which equality and balance are achieved, and that is the Balance. It is known that the Book, which encompasses the divine commands, and the instrument set for dealing equitably, can only be preserved, for the common folk to follow them, by the sword, which is the proof of Allah against whoever denies, is obstinate, and withdraws his hand from the community's pledge; and it is iron, which has been described as having great might.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 57, verse 26:

﴿And We certainly sent Noah and Abraham﴾, singled out for mention because they are the two fathers of the prophets, peace be upon them,

﴿and placed in their offspring﴾, that is, their children,

﴿prophethood and the Book﴾, that is, revelation. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "the writing with the pen." It is said "kataba kitaban wa kitabatan" (he wrote a writing, and writing).

﴿So among them﴾, that is, among the offspring, or among those to whom they were sent, the mention of sending and of those sent having indicated them,

﴿there is one who is guided, and many of them are defiant transgressors﴾. This is a detail of their condition: that is, among them is the one who was guided by following the messengers, and among them is the one who transgressed, that is, departed from obedience. And dominance belongs to the transgressors.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 57, verse 27:

﴿Then We sent, following in their footsteps,﴾ that is: Nuh, Ibrahim, and those prophets who passed before them,

﴿Our messengers. And We sent after them Isa son of Maryam, and We gave him the Injil, and We placed in the hearts of those who followed him kindness﴾, affection, and gentleness,

﴿and mercy﴾, compassion toward their brethren, as He said describing the companions of the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿compassionate among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. ﴿And monasticism, which they invented﴾, it is their withdrawal to the mountains, fleeing from tribulation in religion and devoting themselves wholly to worship. It is the act attributed to the monks (al-Ruhban, sing. rahib), meaning the one who fears, on the pattern fa'lan from rahiba, like khashyan from khashiya. Its accusative case is governed by a implied verb which the apparent one explains, its estimated form being: "and they invented a monasticism which they invented", that is, they brought it forth from their own selves and vowed to it.

﴿We did not prescribe it for them﴾, We did not impose it upon them,

﴿except seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾. This is an exceptive clause of disconnected type (istithna' munqati'), meaning: but they invented it seeking the pleasure of Allah.

﴿But they did not observe it with its due observance﴾, as it is obligatory upon the one who vows to observe his vow, for it is a covenant with Allah whose breaking is not permitted.

﴿So We gave those among them who believed their reward﴾, that is, the people of kindness and mercy who followed Isa, peace be upon him, or those who believed in Muhammad ﷺ.

﴿And many of them are defiant transgressors﴾, that is, disbelievers.

O you who have believed, the address is to the People of the Book.

Fear Allah and believe in His Messenger, Muhammad (ﷺ),

He will give you, Allah,

a double portion (kiflayn), meaning two shares,

of His mercy, because of your belief in Muhammad (ﷺ) and your belief in those who came before him,

and He will make for you, on the Day of Resurrection,

a light by which you walk, which is the light mentioned in His saying: ﴿Their light will run before them﴾ [al-Hadid: 12], and so on to the end of the verse,

and He will forgive you, your sins,

and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.

{ liam ya'lama } — "so that": li-yaʿlama, "that he may know" (the lam here is the lam of purpose).

﴿That the People of the Book may know﴾: alladhīna lam yuslimū, "those who have not embraced Islam."

And "lā" is redundant (zā'idah).

﴿That they have no power over anything of the bounty of Allah﴾: "an" is the lightened form of the heavy (muthaqqalah) "anna," whose original form is "annahu lā yaqdirūna," meaning that the matter is that they have no power—

﴿over anything of the bounty of Allah﴾, i.e., they will not attain anything of what has been mentioned of the bounty of Allah: of the double portion, the light, and the forgiveness, because they did not believe in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so their faith in those before him did not benefit them, and it never earned them any bounty at all.

﴿And that the bounty﴾: this is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "an lā yaqdirūna" (that they have no power).

﴿is in the hand of Allah﴾, i.e., in His dominion and disposal.

﴿He gives it to whom He wills﴾, from among His servants.

﴿And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾
